title: 5 Stupidly Simple Habits That Made Me a Better Leader
author: The Good Boss
summary: Gaurav Jain says the biggest changes in his leadership over two decades came from five habits so simple he almost dismissed them. He wrote down one leadership win each day to build reflection and self-awareness, and began 1:1s with the question what do you need from me. He stopped replying to messages instantly and built in focus hours, which taught his team to think for themselves and modeled boundaries. He repeated the team's top three priorities constantly until people quoted them back, and he celebrated boring progress such as a smooth meeting or a process that ran without reminders. The argument is that small, unglamorous, repeated behaviors shape trust, clarity and motivation more than big strategic interventions.
points: A daily one-line record of a leadership win builds reflection, a skill most leaders skip, and a store of examples for coaching and reviews.
Asking what do you need from me turns 1:1s from status checks into support and invites candor.
Instant replies train a team to depend on the leader, while focus hours give people room to solve problems and model healthy boundaries.
Repeating three team priorities in many formats makes them the basis for the team's own trade-offs.
Celebrating ordinary progress builds trust and momentum, because ordinary is where trust lives.
quotes: I’ve been leading for more than two decades, and what made the biggest difference in how I lead didn’t come from a fancy MBA course or a breakthrough strategy session.
The point wasn’t to brag or keep score. The point was to reflect. And reflection, as it turns out, is the superpower most leaders skip.
I built in “focus hours” where I didn’t check messages or emails. I turned off Slack notifications, and gave myself (and my team) some breathing space.
And ironically, doing this helped me to gain more respect from my team. When I modeled boundaries, my team members felt safe to set them too.
Then I realized something: If I wasn’t repeating it, no one remembered it.
The world today is full of noise, and clarity is kindness. And clarity comes from repetition.
